head: 73b2feae3779c5ccf769da946aaf89a3814baf72
prompt:
# Routing: a live operator policy layer, editable without a restart

## Why
The routing policy is read once, when the daemon starts. `DEFAULT_POLICY` comes from code and `routing/policy.json` is the eval-generated overlay; both are held in `readonly` Router fields (`src/app.ts`, `src/router/router.ts`). Changing a role's chain or fallbacks therefore means a PR and a deploy. The operator needs to reroute live, above all when a subscription is close to exhaustion, and to keep evals as the source of the recommended defaults. Provider enable/disable is the precedent: it is stored in SQLite, applied in memory at once, and pushed over SSE. This is part 2 of runtime routing configuration. Part 1 (per-run model chains) is independent; parts 3 (discovery and runtime catalog) and 4 (Setup tab) build on this one.

## What
1. **Three layers, merged cell by cell.** Code `DEFAULT_POLICY`, then `routing/policy.json` (evals), then a new **operator layer** stored in SQLite. Each operator entry replaces one `role.cell` (`default`, `trivial`, `small`, `medium`, `large`), exactly as `overlayPolicy` merges today. An additive migration creates:
   - the current operator cells (role, cell, groups JSON, note, updated_at, updated_by);
   - an append-only change history (old value, new value, note, at, by).
2. **Validation** is the same as the startup policy check, with every entry resolved against the current catalog (`validatePolicy` and `transportError` in `src/router/targets.ts`). Reject with a message that names the entry: an unknown or retired id (give the reason); a transport invalid for the role; an unsupported effort; an empty chain; an unknown role or cell.
3. **No restart.** The Router's effective policy can be swapped at runtime, e.g. `router.setPolicy(merged)` behind a single source of truth. Startup builds the merged policy from all three layers.
   - **In-flight runs pick up a change at their next model call**, which is what rerouting around an exhausted subscription needs.
   - **Sticky implementers:** if the operator's new cell no longer contains a run's current implementer, its next implement round routes from the new cell instead of staying on the removed model. Escalation constraints (`minTier`, `exclude` tried) still apply over the new cell.
   - A run's own model chains (part 1, if present) still win over every layer.
   - Each change is published over SSE (a `routing` message) and recorded in history.
4. **Runtime `prefer`.** The operator layer may also hold a provider preference list that replaces `[routing] prefer` from config.toml while it is set. It is validated against known provider ids, and an entry that is a model id or a retired id is rejected (see #344).
5. **Preview.** `GET /api/routing/preview?role=&complexity=` returns the candidates the router would consider right now: in order, each with an eligible/skipped flag and its skip reason (disabled, unhealthy, exhausted until …, over reserve, circuit open, transport). It must have no side effects: no `lastRoute` update and no slot claims.
6. **API** (auth and mutation checks exactly as for `/api/providers/:id/enable`):
   - `GET /api/routing` returns `{ layers: { code, evals, operator }, effective, prefer, history }`. For each effective cell it gives the layer it came from, and the evals cell where the operator overrides it.
   - `PUT /api/routing/cells/:role/:cell` with `{ groups, note? }`, and `DELETE` on the same path (reset to the evals/code value).
   - `PUT` and `DELETE` `/api/routing/prefer`.
7. **CLI.**
   - `limitless routing show [--role r]`: effective cells, each with its layer.
   - `limitless routing set <role>.<cell> <chain> [--note …]`, with the chain written in the run `--model` syntax (comma-separated entries, `|` alternatives, `@effort`).
   - `limitless routing reset <role>.<cell> | --all`.
   - `limitless routing preview <role> [<complexity>]`.
8. **Docs.** GUIDE.md routing section: the three layers, how a live edit relates to `eval policy --write`, and how to reroute around a depleted subscription. Fix the stale lines: GUIDE.md says the overlay overrides only `triage.default`, and that provider cards are on the Dashboard.

## Non-goals
Adding catalog models at runtime, discovery and the Setup tab are later parts. `eval policy --write` keeps writing the reviewed `routing/policy.json`.

## Tests (fakes only)
- Setting an operator cell changes the next `route()` result without a new Router or a restart, and an in-flight fake run's next implement invocation uses it.
- Removing the current implementer from the cell moves the next round off it.
- Reset restores the evals value, and then the code value.
- Validation rejects each bad entry listed above, with its message.
- History records old and new values.
- Preview lists skip reasons and leaves router state unchanged.
- Runtime `prefer` overrides config and is cleared by `DELETE`.
- The operator layer survives a daemon restart (the Store is reopened).
- The migration is additive.

Budget: about 350 changed source lines, plus tests.

Tracking issue: #373.

The test 'startup validates persisted operator cells…' asserts this throw, which locks in the behavior.

The catalog changes routinely: models get retired into REMOVED_MODELS, config.toml models or providers get removed, and parts 3/4 make it runtime-driven. A cell that was valid when set can therefore brick the next

variants.title: Any routing edit cancels every queued or about-to-start invocation in every role
variants.detail: policyRevision is a single global signal. Any setPolicy or setPreferProviders call aborts it, even for an unrelated role or cell. Every run waiting for a slot, or between invocation creation and the model call, then reroutes. Runs in the second case also get a 'cancelled' invocation row with 'routing changed before model call'. That adds noise to invocation history and stats, and the run can lose its place in the provider queue.

variants.title: Any routing edit aborts every pending slot wait for every role and discards its queue position
variants.detail: `router.policyRevision` is a single global AbortController, aborted by every `setPolicy` and `setPreferProviders` call. Each invocation that is waiting for admission, preflight or the pre-call window therefore aborts, releases its place, clears `busy` and calls `route()` again. This happens even when the edit touched an unrelated role or cell (e.g. chat.default). With a contended provider, every edit sends all waiting runs to the back of the FIFO queue. A newer waiter can then overtake older ones, and a waiter already admitted between routing and the model call has its invocation row marked 'cancelled'.

variants.title: Any routing edit aborts every waiting slot acquisition in every run, including unrelated roles
variants.detail: `router.policyRevision` is a single global AbortController. It is aborted on every setPolicy, whatever cell changed, and on every setPreferProviders. Each run that is queued in tracker.acquire/acquireFirst is aborted and re-routed, and it loses its place in the provider queue. An edit to `triage.trivial` therefore reshuffles queued implement and review calls on the same providers, and they rejoin at the back of the queue.

variants.title: Validation errors are raw zod issue JSON dumps
variants.detail: `groups()` wraps `String(error)` from zod, so API and CLI users get a multi-line JSON array of issues (as seen in the probe output `implement.medium: [ {...`). The message does name the cell, and the inner message carries the reason, but this is hard to read in the CLI.

variants.title: Existing config-cache test fails on both base and HEAD
variants.detail: Command: bun test test/git-integrity.test.ts --test-name-pattern 'an unchanged worktree lists its config once'. Output: Expected length: 1; Received length: 2. The identical assertion fails on base commit 0de5e94, so this is not a routing regression.

variants.title: `eval policy` now diffs the proposed overlay against a 'current' policy that includes operator overrides
variants.detail: `evalPolicy()` returns `policy: this.policy`, which now comes from `router.getPolicy()` and includes the SQLite operator layer. `limitless eval policy` prints `policyDiff(data.policy, overlayPolicy(DEFAULT_POLICY, proposed))`. Every live operator override therefore shows up as a change that `--write` would make, although writing policy.json has no effect on those cells while the overrides exist. This misleads review of the eval recommendation.

variants.title: `Factory.policy` now includes operator overrides, so the `eval policy` diff is misleading
variants.detail: `factory.policy` now returns the Router's effective policy, operator layer included. `evalReport` returns it as `policy`, and `src/cli/eval.ts:75` calls `policyDiff(data.policy, overlayPolicy(DEFAULT_POLICY, proposed))`, labelling the output 'current effective → proposed effective'. For any cell the operator overrides, the diff shows a change from the operator value to the eval value. In reality, writing policy.json would not change that cell's effective routing, because the operator layer still wins. It can also report a change when the overlay itself is unchanged.

variants.title: Resetting a cell with no override still writes a history entry and sends an SSE message
variants.detail: `writeRouting(key, null, …)` always inserts a history row and `setCell` always publishes, even when no operator cell existed. Repeated resets of a cell without an override fill the append-only history with null→null entries.

variants.title: Resetting a cell with no operator override still writes a history row and publishes an SSE change
variants.detail: `setCell(role, cell, null)` always calls `writeRouting`, even when no operator row exists. It records an (old null → new null) history entry, invalidates the routing revision (which aborts waiting admissions in every in-flight invoke), and publishes a `routing` message. `GET /api/routing` also returns the whole unbounded history on every call.

# Quota: a configured "unlimited" state instead of unknown

## Why
At work, Claude and Codex run through enterprise CLI logins with effectively no token limit, and may report no rate-limit windows at all. Limitless reads "no windows observed" as *unknown*:
- The shadow review panel skips with "quota headroom is unknown" (src/pipeline/review-shadow.ts:36, :57), so panel evidence is never collected at work.
- The provider card and `limitless providers` show no quota state. A configured "no limit" can't be told apart from missing telemetry.

The work plan says "no limit or no telemetry" must be a normal, configurable state, never a reason to skip.

## What
1. **A provider setting:** `[providers.<id>] quota = "unlimited"`. The other value, `"windows"`, is the default and today's behaviour. An unlimited provider:
   - always has headroom 1, and reserves don't gate it;
   - is never "unknown";
   - still records and shows observed windows, for information only.
   A quota rejection from the CLI still marks it exhausted until the reset: a real rejection always wins.
2. **The shadow panel's check uses the setting.** Unlimited providers pass it. A default provider with no telemetry still skips, as today.
3. **Display.** The UI provider card and `limitless providers` show "No limit (configured)". Quota alerts don't fire for an unlimited provider's windows.
4. **Validation.** Any other value fails config loading with a message that names it.

Coordinate with #318 (config-defined providers), which reshapes provider config. Use whichever provider table exists when this runs.

## Acceptance
- With `quota = "unlimited"` on a provider and no windows observed, the shadow panel runs. Without the setting, it skips with "unknown".
- With a 99% window observed, `headroom()` is 1 for an unlimited provider. A quota-rejected result still marks it exhausted until the reset.
- `quota = "lots"` fails config loading, naming the value.

Budget: about 80 changed source lines plus tests.

Tracking issue: #355.

head: 18dbf9357c5045e15d8563e4ed4e314388b23a67
prompt:
# Runs: per-run model chains for any role

## Why
New models arrive all the time. Trying one today means a catalog or policy change and a deploy, and a run can't be told "use model X for implement". The operator wants to try any catalog model on any role for a single run, look at the result, and only then decide whether a full eval is worth it. Evals still decide the defaults; this makes one-off experiments cheap. It is part 1 of runtime routing configuration (the others: live routing policy, model discovery and runtime catalog additions, a Setup tab).

## What
1. **Request field.** `CreateRunRequest.models?: Partial<Record<Role, string[]>>`. Each value is a chain in policy-cell syntax: ordered groups, `a|b` alternatives within a group, an optional `@effort` per entry, exactly as `DEFAULT_POLICY` cells are written. The roles that can be overridden are the ones a run invokes: triage, spec, holdout, implement, review, verify.
   - **Validate at creation**, with the same rules startup applies to policy cells (`validatePolicy` and `transportError` in `src/router/targets.ts`, plus effort support). Reject with a 400 that names the offending entry: an unknown id; a retired id (give the removal reason); a transport that can't serve the role; an unsupported effort; an unknown role.
   - **Persist it** in a new additive migration column (e.g. `runs.models_json`). `retryRun` carries it over. The retry endpoint (`POST /api/runs/:id/retry`) accepts an optional replacement `models` map, so "retry with a different model" is one call.
2. **Routing.** When a run has a chain for a role, it replaces that role's policy cell, for every complexity, for the whole run.
   - The production reviewer follows the `review` chain. The shadow review panel is unaffected.
   - **Strict, with no silent fallback.** If no candidate in the chain can run (disabled, unhealthy, quota-exhausted or over reserve, circuit open, model rejected, or every one already tried), the stage must NOT fall back to the policy. The run goes to needs_human with a question that names the role, the chain, and each candidate's skip reason. The operator recovers by retrying with another chain, or by resolving the run. To allow fallback, the operator lists fallbacks in the chain itself.
   - **Escalation stays inside the chain.** Implement escalation (after `ROUNDS_PER_IMPLEMENTER` rounds; `minTier`/`exclude` in `src/pipeline/engine.ts`) moves to the next untried candidate in the run's chain, never to a model outside it. When the chain is used up, the run goes to needs_human as above.
   - **An explicit chain wins over the soft vendor-independence rules:** review avoiding the implementer's vendor; holdout avoiding the spec author's vendor; verify avoiding the implementer's vendor and checkpoint. When that happens, record a warning event, e.g. "review used the implementer's vendor (openai) because this run pinned it".
3. **Surfaces.**
   - CLI: `limitless run … --model <role>=<chain>`, repeatable; entries comma-separated, groups `|`-joined (e.g. `--model implement=omlx/qwen-flash@high --model review=claude/opus,codex/sol`). Also `limitless retry <run> [--model …]`, if a retry command exists; otherwise add one.
   - MCP: `create_run` takes `models`.
   - UI New Run form: an optional, collapsed "Models" section with one chain field per role and inline validation errors from the API.
   - Run detail: show the run's model chains.
4. **Visibility.**
   - `limitless show` prints the chains.
   - The PR report's routing section lists them and labels the run a model experiment.
   - The stage summary says when a pinned chain was used.
   - Invocations already record the model actually used; keep it that way.

## Non-goals
Live editing of the global policy, model discovery, adding catalog models at runtime, and the Setup tab are separate issues. Evals are unchanged.

## Tests (fake harness only; no network, no real models)
- A run with `implement: ["<model B>"]` invokes B for implement while the policy names A.
- With B disabled, the run goes to needs_human naming B and its reason, and no other model is invoked for implement.
- With a two-entry chain, escalation moves to the second entry and never leaves the chain.
- An explicit review chain on the implementer's vendor is honoured, with a warning event.
- Validation rejects each of: an unknown id, a retired id (with its reason), a transport invalid for the role, an unsupported effort and an unknown role.
- Retry carries the chains over; retry with a replacement map uses the new chain.
- The migration is additive, and the previous release still opens the database.

Budget: about 250 changed source lines (the UI form included), plus tests.

Tracking issue: #372.

# Resume: record trusted Git paths for worktrees created before #323

## What happened (2026-10-04, deploying #323)
After the restart onto #323, every run whose worktree had been created by the previous release failed on its next git call with `Missing trusted Git paths`:
- 3 fix runs failed;
- 1 needs_human run failed at delivery after its work was done.

#323's hardened wrapper (`trustedEnv`, src/git/command.ts) refuses a linked worktree without a `<worktree>.git-paths` record. Only `createWorktree` writes that record, so worktrees made before the upgrade never get one. The same check broke `scripts/land-pr.sh`'s private check in linked worktrees; that is fixed on #316's branch.

The work wasn't lost: the commits sat in the worktrees and were salvaged by hand.

## Fix
- When a run resumes and its worktree is a linked worktree with no record, record it once (`recordWorktree`). Log that this happened.
  - An agent confined by #323 can't delete the record, because the record sits outside the writable checkout. So a missing record means the worktree predates the upgrade.
  - The resumed run gets no less trust than it had before the upgrade.
- Alternatively, record every existing worktree from a migration step at daemon start.

## Acceptance
- A run whose worktree has no record is parked, then resumed under the new code. It finishes, with exactly one "recorded legacy worktree" log line.
- A worktree whose record exists but no longer matches still fails closed ("Unsafe worktree Git administration").

Budget: ≤ 20 changed source lines plus a test. Low priority: on this machine every affected run has been handled. It matters for the next install that upgrades with runs in flight.

Tracking issue: #357.

Before this change, a needs_human run went straight back to needs_human. Now any git or trust failure in its worktree marks the run 'failed', which loses the human-review state. variants.detail: The request asks for a single recordWorktree call on resume, or a migration step, within 20 source lines. It also adds a DB column, a time-based SQL heuristic and two store methods. This duplicates and diverges from trustedEnv/recordWorktree in src/git/command.ts. For example, it rejects config files that trustedEnv allows in the admin dir, and it adds a uid check. Future changes now have two sources of truth to keep in sync.

# CI failures: classify deterministically and rerun transient ones

## Why
docs/research/12 §0 and §4.2: of 16 failed CI runs on factory branches, only 3 were fixable in the PR's own code. The rest:
- 7 environment or version differences;
- 2 caused by main moving;
- 2 flaky;
- 2 infrastructure.

Today a red CI emits `pr.ci_failed`, and the orchestrator reruns or investigates by hand. On 2026-10-04 a smoke-test flake blocked a land until it was rerun by hand. The gates already re-run timed-out checks locally (#311, and post-merge in #347); CI has no equivalent.

## What (the first slice: deterministic only, no model)
1. **Classify each `pr.ci_failed` on a factory PR.** Fetch the failing check runs and jobs by REST, only when the GraphQL state changed. Then decide:
   - **Main is red on the same check:** pause per-PR reactions for that check, and emit one `ci.main_red` item for the repository.
   - **Transient:** a job timed out or failed to start, a run was cancelled without being superseded by a newer push, or a test hit its own timeout ("timed out after"). Rerun the failed jobs once at the same SHA.
   - **Anything else:** emit `ci.needs_fix` with the failure signature. This slice takes no further action.
2. **A flake ledger.** A new table (additive migration) records each failure signature: check name, the failing test or error line, and the runner image. It also records SHA and outcome. A rerun that passes at the same SHA is the only evidence of nondeterminism that counts. The ledger never quarantines a test, and never touches security tests.
3. **Caps and controls.** At most one rerun per PR, SHA and signature. A config switch turns reruns off.
4. **Untrusted input.** Log excerpts in feed items are quoted data, and are never followed as instructions.

Out of scope, for follow-ups:
- the formatter autofix;
- local reproduction on the head and on the merge;
- model-driven fix rounds on the same PR (#351);
- conflict rounds (#46).

## Acceptance (fake `gh` fixtures)
- A timed-out job is rerun once. If the rerun passes, a ledger row records the flake. If it fails again, the result is `ci.needs_fix` with no second rerun.
- With main red on the same check, there is no per-PR rerun and one `ci.main_red` item.
- A run cancelled by a newer push is not rerun.
- A log excerpt containing instructions appears quoted in the feed item.

Budget: about 250 changed source lines plus tests.

Related: #311, #347, #352 (the landing queue, which waits on this for transient failures), docs/research/12 §4.2.

Tracking issue: #353.

# CI failures: classify deterministically and rerun transient ones

## Why
docs/research/12 §0 and §4.2: of 16 failed CI runs on factory branches, only 3 were fixable in the PR's own code. The rest:
- 7 environment or version differences;
- 2 caused by main moving;
- 2 flaky;
- 2 infrastructure.

Today a red CI emits `pr.ci_failed`, and the orchestrator reruns or investigates by hand. On 2026-10-04 a smoke-test flake blocked a land until it was rerun by hand. The gates already re-run timed-out checks locally (#311, and post-merge in #347); CI has no equivalent.

## What (the first slice: deterministic only, no model)
1. **Classify each `pr.ci_failed` on a factory PR.** Fetch the failing check runs and jobs by REST, only when the GraphQL state changed. Then decide:
   - **Main is red on the same check:** pause per-PR reactions for that check, and emit one `ci.main_red` item for the repository.
   - **Transient:** a job timed out or failed to start, a run was cancelled without being superseded by a newer push, or a test hit its own timeout ("timed out after"). Rerun the failed jobs once at the same SHA.
   - **Anything else:** emit `ci.needs_fix` with the failure signature. This slice takes no further action.
2. **A flake ledger.** A new table (additive migration) records each failure signature: check name, the failing test or error line, and the runner image. It also records SHA and outcome. A rerun that passes at the same SHA is the only evidence of nondeterminism that counts. The ledger never quarantines a test, and never touches security tests.
3. **Caps and controls.** At most one rerun per PR, SHA and signature. A config switch turns reruns off.
4. **Untrusted input.** Log excerpts in feed items are quoted data, and are never followed as instructions.

Out of scope, for follow-ups:
- the formatter autofix;
- local reproduction on the head and on the merge;
- model-driven fix rounds on the same PR (#351);
- conflict rounds (#46).

## Acceptance (fake `gh` fixtures)
- A timed-out job is rerun once. If the rerun passes, a ledger row records the flake. If it fails again, the result is `ci.needs_fix` with no second rerun.
- With main red on the same check, there is no per-PR rerun and one `ci.main_red` item.
- A run cancelled by a newer push is not rerun.
- A log excerpt containing instructions appears quoted in the feed item.

Budget: about 250 changed source lines plus tests.

Related: #311, #347, #352 (the landing queue, which waits on this for transient failures), docs/research/12 §4.2.

Tracking issue: #353.

Consequently, a permitted transient rerun can automatically rerun a downstream security job, violating the security-test exclusion.

Output: `AssertionError: Jobs containing security tests must not be rerun`, with actual `["repos/o/r/actions/jobs/21/rerun

variants.title: Exclude jobs containing successful security steps from reruns
variants.detail: Security step names are checked only when the step failed. Rerunning an Actions job repeats its successful steps too, so a mixed job containing successful security tests and a later timeout passes this guard and reruns the security tests. A direct classifier probe with a successful step named "Security tests" produced reruns=1 and outcome="rerunning", contrary to the requirement to never touch security tests.

variants.title: Recognize test timeout diagnostics beyond Bun and Playwright
variants.detail: The anchored timeout expression excludes legitimate test-owned timeout messages such as Node's `test timed out after 100ms`. These failures are classified as needing a fix instead of receiving the requested transient retry. Command: `bun /private/tmp/lr-pKEV2z/claude-501/review-ci.ts`. Output: `Node test timeout result: {"posts":0,"outcome":"failed","needsFix":1}`.

variants.title: Resolve definitively rejected reruns instead of waiting forever
variants.detail: The rerun is claimed before the POST, but every non-201 response throws without resolving that claim. If GitHub explicitly rejects the request, subsequent inspections see run_attempt unchanged and retain rerun_requested indefinitely, emitting no ci.needs_fix. Command: bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review.test.ts". Output: after explicit HTTP 403: {"outcomes":["rerun_requested"],"feed":[]}; assertion Expected: true, Received: false.

variants.title: The feed excerpt is the first 2000 characters of the raw job log, which is usually runner setup boilerplate
variants.detail: `emit(..., log || f.line)` quotes `excerpt.trim().slice(0, 2000)`. GitHub Actions logs begin with runner, image and checkout setup output, so for real failures the excerpt rarely contains the failing line. The signature line is extracted separately, but the excerpt adds little diagnostic value.

variants.title: needs_fix excerpt is the first 2000 characters of the job log, which is runner preamble
variants.detail: `emit(..., log || f.line)` passes the full log, and `excerpt.trim().slice(0, 2000)` keeps its head. GitHub Actions logs open with runner version, OS, runner image, token permissions and checkout setup. Those easily exceed 2000 characters, so the quoted excerpt almost never contains the failure the orchestrator needs to see.

variants.title: Failure signature uses the first line that loosely matches error/fail, including volatile durations
variants.detail: The signature line is the first log line that matches `\b(error|fail(ed|ure)?)\b`. Setup noise can match first. The chosen line can also carry run-specific data, as in the test fixture `(fail) slow [5000.01ms]`. The same flake then produces different signatures across runs, which weakens the ledger's purpose of recording each failure signature.

variants.title: Failure signature includes volatile text such as test durations, so the same flake gets a different signature on each run
variants.detail: `ciSignature` takes the first log line matching error or fail verbatim (only the timestamp is stripped). For Bun that line is '(fail) slow [5000.01ms]', which includes the measured duration. variants.title: Signature line and feed excerpt come from the start of the log, not the failure
variants.detail: ciSignature picks the first line anywhere in the log that matches error/fail. That can be setup output, or a passing test whose name contains 'error' or 'failed' (runners such as jest --verbose, pytest -v and go test -v print passing test names). The feed excerpt is `excerpt.trim().slice(0, 2000)` of the full log (lines 324 and 507). That is the runner preamble (runner version, OS, image, token permissions), not the failing output. Durations embedded in the line (e.g. `[5000.01ms]`) also make the same flake produce a different signature on each run.

variants.title: Paused (main-red) PRs are fully re-inspected over REST on every poll

variants.detail: The main-red branch continues before job/log inspection and recordCiFailure, so these failures never enter the ledger. Pausing per-PR reactions should not discard the requested failure history. Command: `bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review.test.ts"`. Output: `main red {"ledger":0,"mainRed":1}`; assertion: `Expected length: 1; Received length: 0`.

variants.title: Main-red failures bypass the failure ledger
variants.detail: The main-red branch continues before fetching job evidence, constructing the failure signature, or recording the ledger row. This loses the requested check/error/runner-image/SHA record for these failures. The isolated probe command above produced main-red: {"ledgerRows":0,"posts":0,"feed":["ci.main_red","ci.main_red"]}. If the checks subsequently recover, the original failure is never recorded.

variants.title: Main-red failures are omitted from the failure ledger
variants.detail: The main-red branch continues before job inspection and recordCiFailure, so these PR failure signatures, SHAs, runner images, and outcomes are never persisted. Pausing reactions should not discard the requested failure history. Command `bun "$TMPDIR/ci-review-probes.ts"` produced `observed main-red ledger rows: 0` and `FAIL main-red PR failures enter the ledger ... 0 !== 1`.

variants.title: Case-sensitive API URL validation rejects valid repositories
variants.detail: Repository registration preserves the user's slug casing, while GitHub returns canonical casing in check_run_url. This strict comparison rejects a legitimate job even though the preceding details_url comparison accepts case differences. The rerun reconciliation prefix check has the same problem. Running `bun "$TMPDIR/ci-review.ts"` with stored `o/r` and returned `O/R` produced `{"name":"canonical-repo-case","posts":0,"outcomes":[],"needsFix":0,"error":"Error: Incomplete failing job"}`.

variants.title: Compare repository names case-insensitively in returned job URLs
variants.detail: The job check_run_url comparison uses the configured repository casing exactly. GitHub repository names are case-insensitive, and returned URLs can use canonical casing. This rejects valid job evidence indefinitely, preventing both classification and reruns. The rerun reconciliation prefix at line 265 has the same issue. Probe: `bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review-probe.test.ts"` used repository `o/r` with returned URL `https://api.github.com/repos/O/R/check-runs/11`. Observed twice: `Incomplete failing job`, with `reruns 0 needs_fix 0`; the rerun assertion failed (Expected length 1, Received length 0).

variants.title: Accept canonical repository casing in check-run URLs
variants.detail: The exact check_run_url comparison rejects valid GitHub responses when the configured repository spelling differs from GitHub's canonical casing. GitHub repository names are case-insensitive, and the surrounding details_url check already accommodates this. Inspection remains pending forever instead of classifying or rerunning the job. Regression command: `bun test /private/tmp/lr-eO88DH/claude-501/ci-review.test.ts`. The casing test failed with `Expected length: 1; Received length: 0` for rerun requests.

variants.title: Reconciliation loses results when a later attempt reruns another job
variants.detail: Reconciliation reads only the workflow's latest attempt. Partial job reruns can leave the originating job's completed result in an earlier attempt while the latest attempt contains another job. The missing name is then treated as ambiguous forever, preventing flake recording and further classification. Command: `bun /private/tmp/lr-sHSr7q/claude-501/ci-review/probe.ts latest`. With the original job succeeding in attempt 2 and another job succeeding in attempt 3, output was `Later unrelated attempt: Ambiguous CI rerun job outcome: rerunning` and `ASSERTION FAILED: a successful rerun in attempt 2 is never read after an unrelated attempt 3`.

variants.title: Later partial attempts strand tracked rerun results
variants.detail: Reconciliation searches only the latest workflow attempt. GitHub partial reruns can omit jobs completed in earlier attempts, so a later rerun of another job makes the tracked job disappear from this query permanently. Every subsequent inspection throws instead of recording its result. Running `bun /private/tmp/lr-MP54Mh/claude-501/ci-review.ts` produced `FAIL a tracked rerun is reconciled after a later partial attempt: Error: Ambiguous CI rerun job`.

variants.title: Search intervening attempts when reconciling a rerun
variants.detail: Reconciliation only searches the workflow's latest attempt. A job-specific rerun does not include unrelated jobs, so a subsequent rerun of another job makes the originating result unreachable. The classifier throws 'Ambiguous CI rerun job' and leaves the ledger pending indefinitely. Command: bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review-repro.test.ts". Output: Expected: "failed_then_passed"; Received: "rerunning"; error: "Error: Ambiguous CI rerun job".

variants.title: Keep newly requested reruns pending until their outcome is observed
variants.detail: pendingRerun is computed before this inspection requests new reruns, so the function can return true immediately after requesting one. The poller clears ciPending and only resumes inspection when ciKey changes. Because GraphQL fetches only 100 contexts, a rerun outside that page can finish without changing ciKey when another check keeps the rollup red. Its ledger outcome then remains rerunning forever. Temporary regression command `bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review.test.ts"` produced `REST calls after invisible rerun: 0` and `Expected: "failed_then_passed" / Received: "rerunning"`.

variants.title: Observe rerun completion beyond the first 100 contexts
variants.detail: An outstanding rerun triggers inspection only when ciChanged is true. The query observes just the first 100 contexts, while REST can discover and rerun checks outside that page. Completion of such a check can leave ciKey unchanged indefinitely. Command: bun test "$TMPDIR/review-ci.test.ts". Output: hidden rerun {"outcome":"rerunning","additionalRestCalls":0}; expected failed_then_passed.

variants.title: Recognize Node test-runner timeout diagnostics
variants.detail: The timeout matcher rejects Node's actual diagnostic, `error: 'test timed out after 10ms'`, so an eligible test timeout emits ci.needs_fix without rerunning. A fixture using captured Node TAP output with GitHub-style timestamps reproduces this. Command: `bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review.test.ts"`. Output: `Node timeout {"reruns":0,"needsFix":1}`; assertion: `Expected length: 1; Received length: 0`.

variants.title: Indented Playwright timeout diagnostics are not classified as transient
variants.detail: The Playwright alternative is anchored without allowing leading whitespace. Standard reporter output such as `    Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded.` therefore produces ci.needs_fix instead of a rerun. Command `bun "$TMPDIR/ci-review-probes.ts"` produced `observed rerun POSTs: 0 needs_fix items: 1` and `FAIL indented Playwright timeout is transient ... 0 !== 1`.

variants.title: Test timeout classification excludes the requested diagnostic
variants.detail: Only three hardcoded diagnostic formats qualify. An actual failure line such as `error: smoke timed out after 30000ms` is classified as needs-fix despite matching the requested test timeout case. The added tests explicitly expect this exclusion. Running `bun "$TMPDIR/ci-review.ts"` produced `{"name":"test-own-timeout","posts":0,"outcomes":["failed"],"needsFix":4,"error":""}`.

variants.title: Playwright security failures can be automatically rerun
variants.detail: Security detection ignores Playwright failure headings such as `1) [chromium] › tests/security.spec.ts:10:1 › rejects unauthorized access`. In a generic job concluded timed_out, that evidence does not prevent recording the failure and rerunning the job. This violates the security-test exclusion. Command `bun "$TMPDIR/ci-review-probes.ts"` produced `observed rerun POSTs: 1 ledger rows: 1` and `FAIL Playwright security timeout never reruns ... 1 !== 0`.

variants.title: Recognize standard security-test failure diagnostics
variants.detail: The security exclusion misses standard Go failure lines such as '--- FAIL: TestSecurity (0.00s)'. A generic timed-out job containing that failure is rerun and entered in the ledger, violating the security-test exclusion. Command: bun test "$TMPDIR/review-ci.test.ts". Output: security reruns {"reruns":1,"ledger":[..."outcome":"rerunning"...]}; assertion expected zero reruns.

variants.title: While main is red or a rerun is pending, the full REST inspection repeats on every poll although GraphQL is unchanged
variants.detail: classifyCi returns false when paused, so ciPending stays true. Every poll then re-fetches the default-branch commit, its checks and statuses, any pending reruns, and the PR checks, against the request's rule of fetching "only when the GraphQL state changed". Returning null also sets complete=false, so a repository access problem cannot clear while main stays red.

variants.title: Persisted main-red pauses bypass the GraphQL-change guard
variants.detail: The request says: “Fetch the failing check runs and jobs by REST, only when the GraphQL state changed.” A main-red pause persists ciPending=true, which re-enters classifyCi on unchanged observations and fetches the failing PR checks again. Command: TMPDIR=/private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501 TMP=/private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501 TEMP=/private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501 bun test /private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501/ci-entry-review.test.ts. The unchanged-GraphQL fixture failed with “Expected: 0” and “Received: 3” additional REST calls.

variants.title: Main-red pause re-fetches REST on every poll, though the request limits fetching to GraphQL changes
variants.detail: When a PR's failing check is red on main, `classifyCi` returns `!paused` = false. `record()` then returns null with `ciPending` still true, so the next poll reclassifies with no GraphQL change. Each pass reads the main commit, main's check-runs and the PR's check-runs. Main's checks are fetched again for every PR rather than once per repository, and this continues for as long as main stays red, possibly hours or days. The request says 'Fetch the failing check runs and jobs by REST, only when the GraphQL state changed.' Because `record` returns null, the mergeability nudge is also skipped and the repository's access-problem clear never runs while paused.

variants.title: Observations are now discarded entirely whenever observePrHead refuses, including while a push is in progress or left stuck
variants.detail: Before this change, record() ignored observePrHead's result and always saved the snapshot and its feed items. Now `if (!store.observePrHead(...)) return undefined;` drops the whole observation whenever the version moved or pushingTo(prUrl) is true. pushingTo stays true until the pushing run is terminal, and the store's own comment says "a crash can leave one behind". During that window the poller never records merges, closes, comments or CI changes for the PR. Only classifyCi needs to be gated on the head being current.

variants.title: record() now drops the whole PR observation when the head epoch check refuses
variants.detail: The base code called `store.observePrHead(pr.url, head, since)` and still saved the snapshot and emitted feed items. The change returns early when that call returns false, which happens while a round is pushing or when the version has moved. During that window pr.merged, pr.closed, review and comment events for the PR are not recorded. This change in behaviour is outside the CI scope and is untested.

variants.title: Poller now drops the whole observation while a round is pushing
variants.detail: `record()` now returns early when `observePrHead(...)` returns false. Before, the snapshot was still saved and feed items such as merged or closed were still emitted. While a round is pushing to the PR, or once the head version has changed since the read, the poller records nothing. This adds a delay, and it is a behaviour change outside the requested scope.

variants.title: Unaccepted rerun requests remain pending forever
variants.detail: A 429, network failure before submission, or crash between claiming and posting leaves outcome rerun_requested. When GitHub never creates another attempt, reconciliation always continues here, and the pending prior record suppresses ci.needs_fix indefinitely. Command: bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review.test.ts". Output: after 100 reconciliation polls {"complete":false,"posts":1,"outcome":"rerun_requested","needsFix":0}; Expected: true, Received: false.

variants.title: Resolve claims when rate limiting rejects the rerun
variants.detail: A rejected HTTP 429 leaves rerun_requested permanently claimed. Because no rerun actually started, run_attempt never advances; reconciliation neither retries nor emits ci.needs_fix. Command: bun test "$TMPDIR/review-ci.test.ts". Output after cooldown and eight further polls: rate-limited claim {"outcome":"rerun_requested","reruns":1,"needsFix":0}; assertion expected outcome not to remain rerun_requested.

variants.title: Lagging check data reports a confirmed passing rerun as needing a fix
variants.detail: Successful reconciliation adds only the new job ID to resolved. If the check-runs endpoint still returns the original failed job, that ID is not skipped. The prior failed_then_passed record prevents another rerun but falls through to needsFix, producing contradictory ledger and feed results. Command: bun test "$TMPDIR/ci-review.test.ts". Output: successful rerun with lagging checks {"outcome":"failed_then_passed","feed":["ci.needs_fix"]}; Expected: false, Received: true.

variants.title: Main-red alerts are deduplicated per check instead of per repository
variants.detail: Each failing check name receives a separate ci.main_red key. When test and lint fail on both main and a PR, two repository items are emitted, contrary to the requested single repository item. Command `bun "$TMPDIR/ci-review-probes.ts"` produced `observed ci.main_red items: 2` and `FAIL one main-red feed item per repository ... 2 !== 1`.

variants.title: Main-branch status lookup depends on the PR's context types
variants.detail: The shared checks function fetches legacy commit statuses only when the PR snapshot contains StatusContext entries or is truncated. Consequently, a failing main status is invisible when the PR exposes the same check through CheckRun. Running `bun "$TMPDIR/ci-review.ts"` with a failing main status named test produced `{"name":"main-red-legacy-status","posts":1,"mainStatusReads":0,"outcomes":["rerunning"],"needsFix":0,"error":""}`.

variants.title: Failures observed after PR closure escape classification
variants.detail: The request says: “Classify each pr.ci_failed on a factory PR” and “Anything else: emit ci.needs_fix with the failure signature.” diffPr can emit pr.ci_failed when an already observed PR closes and its pending CI finishes red, but this OPEN-only guard skips classification. Command: TMPDIR=/private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501 TMP=/private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501 TEMP=/private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501 bun test /private/tmp/lr-nHrYHx/claude-501/ci-entry-review.test.ts. The closure fixture confirmed one pr.ci_failed, then failed its classification assertion with “Expected: > 0” and “Received: 0”.

variants.title: A rerun that ends with a conclusion other than success or a failure stays pending forever
variants.detail: In the loop that resolves pending reruns, a completed job whose conclusion is neither `success` nor in `bad` hits `else continue`. Examples are `neutral` or `skipped`, or a failure while main is red on that check. The row stays `rerunning`. When the rollup is SUCCESS, `classifyCi` keeps returning false because a pending rerun exists, so `record()` returns null on every poll. That means repeated REST inspection and `complete = false` for the repository.

variants.title: Feed excerpt is the start of the job log, not the failure
variants.detail: `emit` is called with `log || f.line`, and the excerpt is `excerpt.trim().slice(0, 2000)`. For GitHub Actions jobs, the first 2000 characters of the raw log are runner setup output (runner version, image details, checkout). The actual failure line is almost never inside the excerpt, so `ci.needs_fix` items show boilerplate. The `signature.line` field does carry the matched line.

variants.title: The needs_fix excerpt is the start of the job log, not the failure
variants.detail: `emit(..., log || f.line)` sets `excerpt = quote(log.trim().slice(0, 2000))`. A real Actions job log starts with runner setup output (runner version, OS, image, checkout), so the first 2000 characters almost never contain the failure. The excerpt is noise, and the failing lines that sit past 2000 characters are dropped.

variants.title: Feed excerpt is the first 2000 chars of the job log (runner setup), not the failure
variants.detail: `emit(..., log || f.line)` passes the whole job log, and `excerpt.trim().slice(0, 2000)` keeps its head. GitHub Actions job logs begin with runner, image and setup output, so for any realistic log the excerpt contains no failure information.

variants.title: Ledger signatures include per-run noise, so the same flake never matches across occurrences
variants.detail: `ciSignature` uses the first log line matching `/timed out after|##[error]|\b(?:error|fail(?:ed|ure)?)\b/i`, verbatim apart from a leading timestamp, as the error line. That keeps volatile content such as Bun's duration suffix. It also matches incidental setup lines (e.g. `fail-fast: true`) that print before the real failure. The flake ledger exists to record each failure signature so recurring nondeterminism can be recognised, and these signatures differ on every occurrence.

variants.title: Failure signature can pick a passing test or setup line, and it includes run timings
variants.detail: `ciSignature` takes the first log line matching `/timed out after|##\[error\]|\b(?:error|fail(?:ed|ure)?)\b/i`. Passing test names containing 'error' or 'fail', and action inputs such as `continue-on-error: false` or `fail-on-cache-miss`, match before the actual failure. Lines also keep durations such as `[5000.01ms]`, so the same failure produces a different signature on every run. The ledger's "failing test or error line" is then wrong, unrelated failures in one job collapse into one signature (the cap is over-applied, and needs_fix items are deduplicated away), and identical failures never aggregate across runs.

variants.title: Ad-hoc '> ' quoting instead of the codebase's untrusted-data convention
variants.detail: Untrusted GitHub text elsewhere goes through `quotedJson`, or is labelled with an explicit 'untrusted … quoted data' preface (`src/integrations/github.ts:48`, `src/pipeline/triage-decisions.ts`). This change adds a separate `> `-prefix scheme plus an `untrusted: true` flag. That satisfies the letter of the requirement but is inconsistent with the existing approach, and it doesn't escape angle brackets or tags if feed data is later embedded in a tagged prompt.

variants.title: The change is roughly twice the stated budget, and classifyCi is a dense single closure
variants.detail: The request budgets about 250 source lines, and the change adds about 530. A single 340-line classifyCi closure mixes main-episode tracking, rerun resolution, security screening, pagination and the rerun POST, with many throw paths.

variants.title: Two migrations for one new, unshipped table; change is about twice the source-line budget
variants.detail: `rerun_job` is added by a second ALTER migration, although the table is created in the same change. The source diff is about 560 lines against a budget of about 250, with a 411-line classifier that is hard to audit.

variants.title: About 580 changed source lines against a budget of about 250
variants.detail: The classifier alone is 411 lines of dense nested closures, and some of its checks are defensive but hard to follow, such as the ambiguous-job, completion-time and annotation-count checks. Each extra throw path adds to the starvation problem above. The request set a budget of about 250 source lines.

variants.title: Second migration alters a table created by this same change
variants.detail: One migration in this unmerged change creates ci_failures and a second migration immediately adds rerun_job to it.

variants.title: Security regex matches unrelated substrings such as 'disaster'
variants.detail: `/…|sast|dast|vulnerab/i` has no word boundaries, so 'disaster', 'podcast' (no) or 'sastisfy'-style tokens count as security evidence. That suppresses both the rerun and the ledger row. The effect is conservative but surprising.

variants.title: Fail-fast cancelled matrix jobs are treated as transient, rerun, and recorded as flakes
variants.detail: Any check or job with conclusion `cancelled` is classified as transient, unless the remote head has moved. The request covers a *run* cancelled without being superseded. In a matrix with fail-fast, a real failure in one job cancels its siblings at the same SHA. Those cancelled siblings get rerun, and when the rerun passes, `failed_then_passed` is written to the ledger as nondeterminism evidence, although nothing was nondeterministic. The rerun budget is also spent for nothing. The test 'eligible cancelled failure reruns only its job' locks this behaviour in.

variants.title: Multiple transient jobs in one run are rerun one by one; later POSTs may be rejected and reported as needs_fix
variants.detail: Each eligible job gets its own POST to `actions/jobs/{id}/rerun`. After the first one, the run is in progress again, and GitHub may refuse a second job rerun on a running run. A 4xx response is treated as a definitive `rerun_rejected` followed by needs_fix. The request says "Rerun the failed jobs", and `runs/{id}/rerun-failed-jobs` does that in one call. I could not verify GitHub's live behaviour here.

prompt:
# Models: discover what providers serve, and add catalog models at runtime

## Why
Catalog models are defined in code or config.toml and read once at startup, and nothing checks what a provider actually serves. A local server's model was replaced and the catalog kept naming the old build. Only a deploy smoke check caught it, and only a code change and a deploy fixed it (#371). The operator wants to add a newly served model in seconds and try it, through a run's model chain or the live policy, without a release. This is part 3 of runtime routing configuration. It depends on part 2 (the live operator policy layer and the runtime-swappable Router).

## What
1. **Discovery.** For providers with an OpenAI-compatible model list, the scheduled health probe (`src/router/providers.ts`, `healthUrl` → `/v1/models`) already fetches that list with authentication. It currently checks only `res.ok`; it should also parse `data[].id`.
   - Store the served ids per provider (additive migration: provider, backend model, first seen, last seen).
   - Expose them in `GET /api/catalog` (below) and in provider status: **served but not in the catalog**, and **in the catalog but not served**.
   - A catalog model that a healthy, discovered provider doesn't serve is skipped by the router with the reason "not served by <provider>". It must not cost an attempt, and it gets a provider-card warning.
   - CLI-backed providers (claude, codex) and OpenRouter are out of scope for discovery here.
2. **Runtime catalog additions.**
   - `POST /api/catalog/models` takes a provider, local id, backend model name, vendor, origin, base origin, tier, supported efforts, default effort, price and notes. Origin is explicit: never defaulted or guessed. Validate with the rules of config.toml's `[[providers.models]]` (`modelSchema` and the merge rules in `src/router/config-catalog.ts`): the id syntax, the effort being in efforts, an existing provider, and no collision with a code or config model.
   - Persist it in SQLite (additive migration), merge it into the Router's model map with no restart, and publish over SSE.
   - `PATCH` and `DELETE` work only on runtime-added models; code and config entries stay read-only. `DELETE` refuses while an operator policy cell names the model, and the error names those cells. A stored run chain that names a deleted model is skipped with a reason, like a retired id.
   - **Containment:** a runtime-added model is never a candidate for implement escalation's `minTier` widening (`src/router/router.ts`) or free-first widening unless a policy cell or a run chain names it explicitly. Experiments must not leak into production routing.
3. **API and CLI.**
   - `GET /api/catalog` returns models with their source (code, config, runtime), plus the discovery results per provider.
   - `limitless catalog list`, `limitless catalog add <provider>/<id> --model <backend> --origin … --vendor … --tier N [--efforts none,high] [--effort …]`, and `limitless catalog remove <id>`.
   - `limitless providers` shows served-not-in-catalog and catalog-not-served.
4. **Smoke.** The deploy smoke check reports a catalog model a reachable provider doesn't serve as a clear failure, naming the model and the served list.
5. **Docs.** GUIDE.md: how to add a newly served local model. The current text says the catalog is built in and config-defined providers are only planned; fix it.

## Tests (fakes only; fake fetch for `/v1/models`)
- Discovery parses served ids and reports both differences.
- A catalog model that isn't served is skipped with its reason, and costs no attempt.
- A runtime add is routable at once via `resolveFor`, a run chain and a live policy cell, without a restart.
- Validation rejects: a missing origin, a bad id, a default effort not in efforts, an unknown provider and a collision.
- `DELETE` is refused while a policy cell references the model.
- A runtime-added high-tier model is not picked by `minTier` escalation unless named.
- Runtime models survive a restart.
- The migrations are additive.

Budget: about 350 changed source lines, plus tests.

Tracking issue: #374. Part 2 (#373) has landed: build on its runtime-swappable Router and operator policy layer.

gold.summary: Catalog mutation can invalidate a shadowed retained policy and prevent the daemon from restarting.

variants.title: Backend corrections retain the old model rejection
variants.detail: Catalog updates leave ProviderTracker.modelBlocks unchanged. A provider rejection blocks the local ID for 24 hours, so correcting its backend name still skips the corrected model. Deleting and re-adding the ID also retains the block. Command: env TMPDIR=/private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501 TMP=/private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501 TEMP=/private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501 bun test /private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501/runtime-catalog-review.test.ts. Output: {"candidates":[],"skipped":[{"modelId":"codex/experiment","reason":"codex: model rejected: bad-build is unsupported"}]}; assertion: Expected length: 1, Received length: 0.

variants.title: Clear stale model rejection blocks when replacing a backend
variants.detail: Catalog mutations update the model map but leave ProviderTracker.modelBlocks untouched. A rejection of the old backend therefore prevents the replacement backend from routing for up to 24 hours. Deleting and re-adding the same ID also retains the block. Reproduction command: bun -e 'import {Store} from "./src/db/store.ts"; import {MODELS,PROVIDERS} from "./src/router/catalog.ts"; import {ProviderTracker} from "./src/router/providers.ts"; import {Router} from "./src/router/router.ts"; import {RuntimeCatalog} from "./src/router/runtime-catalog.ts"; const s=new Store(":memory:"), m=[], t=new ProviderTracker(PROVIDERS,s,{},{}), r=new Router(t,{},m), c=new RuntimeCatalog(s,m,PROVIDERS,r,t); c.add

variants.title: Clear stale model rejection blocks when replacing a backend
variants.detail: Catalog mutations update model definitions but leave ProviderTracker.modelBlocks keyed by the unchanged catalog ID. After a backend rejection, correcting its backend through PATCH still leaves the corrected model unroutable for up to 24 hours. Deleting and re-adding that ID also retains the block. An in-memory add → blockModel → patch → route check printed `resolved backend: good-build` followed by `{"candidates":[],"skipped":[{"modelId":"codex/experiment","reason":"codex: model rejected: unknown model bad-build"}]}`.

variants.title: PATCH cannot clear a default effort
variants.detail: The merge preserves the old effort when omitted, while null and "default" fail validation. Consequently, no JSON PATCH can return an existing model to an unset default effort. This matters for local Claude-backed agent roles, which reject explicit efforts. Command: env TMPDIR=/private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501 TMP=/private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501 TEMP=/private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501 bun test /private/tmp/lr-U5IH6O/claude-501/runtime-catalog-review.test.ts. Output: error: model.effort: invalid or missing field; (fail) PATCH can clear an optional default effort for agent roles.

variants.title: Allow PATCH to clear an optional default effort
variants.detail: Omitting effort preserves the old value, while sending null fails validation. Consequently, an existing runtime model cannot be updated to use backend-default effort, which is needed for Claude-backed agent roles. Direct reproduction command: bun -e 'import {RuntimeCatalog} from "./src/router/runtime-catalog.ts"; import {MODELS,PROVIDERS} from "./src/router/catalog.ts"; const m={...MODELS[0],id:"claude/exp",source:"runtime",effort:"high",supportedEfforts:["high"]}; const c=new RuntimeCatalog({},[m],PROVIDERS,{getPolicy:()=>({})},{}); try {c.patch(m.id,{effort:null});} catch(e) {console.log(String(e));}' Output: Error: model.effort: invalid or missing field

variants.title: PATCH cannot clear a runtime model's default effort
variants.detail: `patch` merges `{...old, ...patch}` and runs the result through `mapFields`. That step drops `undefined` but keeps `null`, and `modelSchema.effort` is `.optional()`, so `{effort: null}` is rejected. JSON has no way to send `undefined`, so a default effort, once set, can only be removed by deleting and re-adding the model. Deletion is itself blocked while any policy cell names the model. GUIDE.md advises omitting the default effort for Claude-backed local servers, so an operator who set one by mistake is stuck.

variants.title: An older probe can overwrite discovery after provider re-enablement
variants.detail: Probe results have no generation or ordering guard. Disabling and re-enabling a provider starts another probe, but the previous probe can finish afterward and replace the newer served list in memory and SQLite. # Models: discover what providers serve, and add catalog models at runtime

## Why
Catalog models are defined in code or config.toml and read once at startup, and nothing checks what a provider actually serves. A local server's model was replaced and the catalog kept naming the old build. Only a deploy smoke check caught it, and only a code change and a deploy fixed it (#371). The operator wants to add a newly served model in seconds and try it, through a run's model chain or the live policy, without a release. This is part 3 of runtime routing configuration. It depends on part 2 (the live operator policy layer and the runtime-swappable Router).

## What
1. **Discovery.** For providers with an OpenAI-compatible model list, the scheduled health probe (`src/router/providers.ts`, `healthUrl` → `/v1/models`) already fetches that list with authentication. It currently checks only `res.ok`; it should also parse `data[].id`.
   - Store the served ids per provider (additive migration: provider, backend model, first seen, last seen).
   - Expose them in `GET /api/catalog` (below) and in provider status: **served but not in the catalog**, and **in the catalog but not served**.
   - A catalog model that a healthy, discovered provider doesn't serve is skipped by the router with the reason "not served by <provider>". It must not cost an attempt, and it gets a provider-card warning.
   - CLI-backed providers (claude, codex) and OpenRouter are out of scope for discovery here.
2. **Runtime catalog additions.**
   - `POST /api/catalog/models` takes a provider, local id, backend model name, vendor, origin, base origin, tier, supported efforts, default effort, price and notes. Origin is explicit: never defaulted or guessed. Validate with the rules of config.toml's `[[providers.models]]` (`modelSchema` and the merge rules in `src/router/config-catalog.ts`): the id syntax, the effort being in efforts, an existing provider, and no collision with a code or config model.
   - Persist it in SQLite (additive migration), merge it into the Router's model map with no restart, and publish over SSE.
   - `PATCH` and `DELETE` work only on runtime-added models; code and config entries stay read-only. `DELETE` refuses while an operator policy cell names the model, and the error names those cells. A stored run chain that names a deleted model is skipped with a reason, like a retired id.
   - **Containment:** a runtime-added model is never a candidate for implement escalation's `minTier` widening (`src/router/router.ts`) or free-first widening unless a policy cell or a run chain names it explicitly. Experiments must not leak into production routing.
3. **API and CLI.**
   - `GET /api/catalog` returns models with their source (code, config, runtime), plus the discovery results per provider.
   - `limitless catalog list`, `limitless catalog add <provider>/<id> --model <backend> --origin … --vendor … --tier N [--efforts none,high] [--effort …]`, and `limitless catalog remove <id>`.
   - `limitless providers` shows served-not-in-catalog and catalog-not-served.
4. **Smoke.** The deploy smoke check reports a catalog model a reachable provider doesn't serve as a clear failure, naming the model and the served list.
5. **Docs.** GUIDE.md: how to add a newly served local model. The current text says the catalog is built in and config-defined providers are only planned; fix it.

## Tests (fakes only; fake fetch for `/v1/models`)
- Discovery parses served ids and reports both differences.
- A catalog model that isn't served is skipped with its reason, and costs no attempt.
- A runtime add is routable at once via `resolveFor`, a run chain and a live policy cell, without a restart.
- Validation rejects: a missing origin, a bad id, a default effort not in efforts, an unknown provider and a collision.
- `DELETE` is refused while a policy cell references the model.
- A runtime-added high-tier model is not picked by `minTier` escalation unless named.
- Runtime models survive a restart.
- The migrations are additive.

Budget: about 350 changed source lines, plus tests.

Tracking issue: #374. Part 2 (#373) has landed: build on its runtime-swappable Router and operator policy layer.

# MCP: review, land and status tools, and a session-start digest

## Why
The MCP server exposes these tools (src/integrations/mcp.ts:227–310):
- create_run, get_run, list_runs, cancel_run;
- answer_question, resolve_run;
- providers;
- feed, feed_ack.

An agent still can't review or land a PR through MCP. A new session also doesn't know what needs attention until it thinks to call the feed. The "new-agent test" in the work plan (a fresh session with only the MCP server) fails at both steps.

## What
1. **Tools.**
   - `limitless_review(run, verdict, reviewedSha, findings)` calls the review-verdict API (#351).
   - `limitless_land(run, sha?)` adds the PR to the land queue (#352).
   - `limitless_status(run)` returns a plain-language state and the next action, derived from the run, its PR observation and its land entry.
2. **A session-start digest.**
   - `limitless digest [--consumer <name>]` prints what needs attention since the consumer's cursor, without acknowledging anything: needs-you runs, PRs waiting for review, blocked lands, and counts.
   - Output is at most 20 lines. Untrusted text (PR titles, comments, CI excerpts) is quoted.
   - The install docs and `limitless init` (#288) offer a Claude Code SessionStart hook that runs it.
3. **Teaching.** The MCP server instructions and a short skill describe the five verbs: submit, inbox/ack, answer, review and status.

## Acceptance
- MCP tests with the fake backend: review and land call the HTTP API with the expected bodies, and API errors become MCP errors.
- The tools-list test includes the new tools and their input schemas.
- With a fixture feed, `digest` prints the counts and top items, never acknowledges, stays within 20 lines, and quotes PR titles.

Budget: about 200 changed source lines plus tests. It needs the review-rounds and landing-queue endpoints first.

Related: #265 (feed), #288 (init/doctor).

Tracking issue: #354. Note: main now has review rounds (#360: limitless review <run> --changes/--approve), the landing queue (#388: limitless land, POST /api/land) and live routing (#378); build the MCP tools on those existing APIs rather than new logic.

# MCP: review, land and status tools, and a session-start digest

## Why
The MCP server exposes these tools (src/integrations/mcp.ts:227–310):
- create_run, get_run, list_runs, cancel_run;
- answer_question, resolve_run;
- providers;
- feed, feed_ack.

An agent still can't review or land a PR through MCP. A new session also doesn't know what needs attention until it thinks to call the feed. The "new-agent test" in the work plan (a fresh session with only the MCP server) fails at both steps.

## What
1. **Tools.**
   - `limitless_review(run, verdict, reviewedSha, findings)` calls the review-verdict API (#351).
   - `limitless_land(run, sha?)` adds the PR to the land queue (#352).
   - `limitless_status(run)` returns a plain-language state and the next action, derived from the run, its PR observation and its land entry.
2. **A session-start digest.**
   - `limitless digest [--consumer <name>]` prints what needs attention since the consumer's cursor, without acknowledging anything: needs-you runs, PRs waiting for review, blocked lands, and counts.
   - Output is at most 20 lines. Untrusted text (PR titles, comments, CI excerpts) is quoted.
   - The install docs and `limitless init` (#288) offer a Claude Code SessionStart hook that runs it.
3. **Teaching.** The MCP server instructions and a short skill describe the five verbs: submit, inbox/ack, answer, review and status.

- MCP tests with the fake backend: review and land call the HTTP API with the expected bodies, and API errors become MCP errors.
- The tools-list test includes the new tools and their input schemas.
- With a fixture feed, `digest` prints the counts and top items, never acknowledges, stays within 20 lines, and quotes PR titles.

Budget: about 200 changed source lines plus tests. It needs the review-rounds and landing-queue endpoints first.

Related: #265 (feed), #288 (init/doctor).

Tracking issue: #354. Note: main now has review rounds (#360: limitless review <run> --changes/--approve), the landing queue (#388: limitless land, POST /api/land) and live routing (#378); build the MCP tools on those existing APIs rather than new logic.

variants.detail: quote() relies on JSON.stringify plus escaping U+007F–U+009F and U+2028/2029. variants.detail: Each row prints the full quoted title and summary; for questions, the summary is replaced with the full open question text. Output from a SessionStart hook goes into the agent's context, so a multi-kilobyte question or a long PR title (untrusted text) produces a very large digest.

variants.title: Digest item lines are unbounded in width
variants.detail: Each row includes the full quoted title and summary. For questions, the summary is replaced with the full open-question text. The output is capped at 20 lines, but a single line can carry kilobytes of untrusted text into every session's context through the SessionStart hook.

variants.title: Historical landing blocks override closed and resolved states

variants.title: Digest lines have no length cap, so 20 lines can still carry a lot of untrusted text
variants.detail: Each row includes the full quoted title and summary, such as question text or a run error. The output stays within 20 lines, but one line can be very long and is injected into the session context at SessionStart.

variants.title: Digest item lines are unbounded in length
variants.detail: Each row quotes the full title and summary. `run.failed` and `run.needs_human` summaries come from `run.error`, and question summaries are the full question text. variants.title: Source changes exceed the requested budget by about 2x
variants.detail: The request set a budget of about 200 changed source lines. The source diff is roughly 400 lines, mostly the detailed status state machine and the digest reconciliation logic. The extra code works but is more to maintain.

variants.title: Fix formatting so the required check passes

variants.title: Do not let an approval hide an active review round
variants.detail: Any matching approval recorded after round creation suppresses the round, including a running or waiting-for-input round. Approval does not stop that work. variants.title: Codex skill tells Codex to use the 'claude' feed consumer
variants.detail: The Codex skill is a byte-for-byte copy of the Claude skill and tells Codex to run `limitless digest --consumer claude`. A Codex session would read, and if it follows the inbox/ack flow acknowledge, the Claude consumer's cursor, so the two agents interfere with each other's inbox.

variants.title: getRunDetail queries the latest approval twice
variants.detail: `approvalFor(prUrl)` already selects the latest review_approvals row. A second, nearly identical query then fetches `created_at` from the same row. variants.title: MCP review verdicts are attributed to reviewer "human"
variants.detail: The MCP review tool strips `reviewer`, and submitReview defaults it to "human". Other paths label their source: the CLI sends `reviewer: $USER`, and the MCP answer tool sends `by: "mcp"`. This breaks the audit trail for who approved a PR before landing.

# MCP: review, land and status tools, and a session-start digest

## Why
The MCP server exposes these tools (src/integrations/mcp.ts:227–310):
- create_run, get_run, list_runs, cancel_run;
- answer_question, resolve_run;
- providers;
- feed, feed_ack.

An agent still can't review or land a PR through MCP. A new session also doesn't know what needs attention until it thinks to call the feed. The "new-agent test" in the work plan (a fresh session with only the MCP server) fails at both steps.

## What
1. **Tools.**
   - `limitless_review(run, verdict, reviewedSha, findings)` calls the review-verdict API (#351).
   - `limitless_land(run, sha?)` adds the PR to the land queue (#352).
   - `limitless_status(run)` returns a plain-language state and the next action, derived from the run, its PR observation and its land entry.
2. **A session-start digest.**
   - `limitless digest [--consumer <name>]` prints what needs attention since the consumer's cursor, without acknowledging anything: needs-you runs, PRs waiting for review, blocked lands, and counts.
   - Output is at most 20 lines. Untrusted text (PR titles, comments, CI excerpts) is quoted.
   - The install docs and `limitless init` (#288) offer a Claude Code SessionStart hook that runs it.
3. **Teaching.** The MCP server instructions and a short skill describe the five verbs: submit, inbox/ack, answer, review and status.

## Acceptance
- MCP tests with the fake backend: review and land call the HTTP API with the expected bodies, and API errors become MCP errors.
- The tools-list test includes the new tools and their input schemas.
- With a fixture feed, `digest` prints the counts and top items, never acknowledges, stays within 20 lines, and quotes PR titles.

Budget: about 200 changed source lines plus tests. It needs the review-rounds and landing-queue endpoints first.

Related: #265 (feed), #288 (init/doctor).

Tracking issue: #354. Note: main now has review rounds (#360: limitless review <run> --changes/--approve), the landing queue (#388: limitless land, POST /api/land) and live routing (#378); build the MCP tools on those existing APIs rather than new logic.
